# eugen_sparse — sparse SwiGLU FFN in Triton

Code only — no model weights.

## Model card summary

## In plain words

A transformer layer spends most of its compute in the feed-forward block, where every token goes through every neuron. Here the neurons are split into small groups, and for each token only the few groups that would respond most strongly are computed — the others are skipped entirely, also when computing gradients. This is a single Python file with GPU kernels written in Triton; it plugs into a PyTorch model in place of a normal SwiGLU feed-forward layer and works with torch.compile .

## Status

Tested experimentally; early observations are promising. It is open whether sparse training pays off over the whole cycle — training from scratch and densifying later (switching the sparse layer to a dense one). The kernel comes from the sparse model variants of the EUGEN project; the production model EUGEN 160M has a dense FFN and does not use it. This is the kernel we trained with (not a simplified demo), cleaned up for publication. Tested on one GPU type only (see Requirements). Not a validated product.

## What it does

- make_subsample_index(d_ff, group_size, samples_per_group, seed) — a fixed random subset of gate rows per group, used to estimate group energy cheaply. Draw once per layer and save it with the model.

- grouped_topk_select(x, W_gate, group_size, num_active_groups, subsample_idx=None, samples_per_group=None, load_balance_bias=None) — for every token, the indices of the num_active_groups groups with the largest energy Σ|SiLU(x·W_gate)| (optionally estimated on the subsample, optionally re-weighted by a balancing bias). Hard top-k, no gradient.

- sparse_swiglu_ffn(x, W_gate, W_up, W_down, group_idx, group_size) — the FFN output Σ_selected (SiLU(x W_g) ⊙ x W_u) W_d with gradients to x and all three weights. Weights in nn.Linear layout. One torch.library.triton_op : no graph breaks under torch.compile .

- update_load_balance_bias(bias, freq_ema, current_freq, target_freq, gamma, bias_max, momentum) — auxiliary-loss-free load balancing (in the style of DeepSeek-V3): call once per optimizer step.

- reference_sparse_swiglu_ffn(...) — a dense masked PyTorch reference with the same math (tests, CPU path).

- kernel_supported(...) , plan(...) — will the Triton path run for this shape, and how the work is split (no GPU work).

## Requirements

- NVIDIA GPU with bf16 tensor cores (Ampere or newer). Tested only on an RTX PRO 6000 (Blackwell); other cards are untested.

- PyTorch with torch.library.triton_op (2.6 or newer per the PyTorch docs; tested on 2.12).

- Triton 3.x (tested on 3.7.0).

- Without a GPU (or with an unsupported shape / older PyTorch) the same math runs on the slow dense reference path. On a CPU you can still check the kernels in the Triton interpreter: TRITON_INTERPRET=1 python test_eugen_sparse.py (needs Triton installed).

## Install

No package to install: copy eugen_sparse.py next to your code (it imports only torch and, if present, triton ).

pip install torch triton # versions as above git clone https://huggingface.co/JakCwi/eugen-sparse

## Quick start

import torch import eugen_sparse as es d_model, d_ff, G, K = 512 , 4096 , 32 , 8 # 8 of 128 groups active = 6.25 % of the neurons dev = "cuda" W_gate = torch.randn(d_ff, d_model, device=dev, dtype=torch.bfloat16) * d_model ** - 0.5 W_up = torch.randn(d_ff, d_model, device=dev, dtype=torch.bfloat16) * d_model ** - 0.5 W_down = torch.randn(d_model, d_ff, device=dev, dtype=torch.bfloat16) * d_ff ** - 0.5 sub, spg = es.make_subsample_index(d_ff, G, samples_per_group= 8 , seed= 0 ) # once per layer sub = sub.to(dev) x = torch.randn( 4096 , d_model, device=dev, dtype=torch.bfloat16) idx = es.grouped_topk_select(x, W_gate, G, K, subsample_idx=sub, samples_per_group=spg) y = es.sparse_swiglu_ffn(x, W_gate, W_up, W_down, idx, G) # [4096, 512] print (es.plan(x.shape[ 0 ], d_model, d_ff, G, K)) # kernel used? token chunks, tiles, determinism

A complete nn.Module ( EugenSparseFFN : subsample and balancing buffers, update_balance() after the optimizer step, autocast, torch.compile ) is in example.py ; python example.py runs on CUDA or, slowly, on CPU.

## Parameters and how to choose them

Layout that worked better for us than several dense layers: first layer dense, the following layers sparse.

## Pitfalls and limitations

- Silent fallback. For an unsupported shape, no Triton or an old PyTorch, the slow dense reference runs instead; on CUDA a one-time warning is printed. Check kernel_supported(...) / plan(...) once.

- The subsample must stay fixed : draw it once per layer, keep it in state_dict . A new draw per step or after resuming changes the selection.

- The balancing bias and its EMA belong to state_dict too ( persistent=True ).

- Non-determinism : y and dX are accumulated with fp32 atomics, so bitwise differences between runs are possible; weight gradients too when there are several token chunks (unless EUGEN_SPARSE_DW_DET=1 ). Selection and the CSR bucketing are deterministic.

- Hard selection : only the selected groups get weight gradients in a step; the routing itself is not learned by gradient.

- group_idx must come from grouped_topk_select (distinct groups per token). Hand-made indices with duplicates or out-of-range values are not checked: the kernel would count a duplicated group twice, the reference once.

- No input validation beyond the shape rules : tokens · num_active_groups must stay below 2³¹ (int32 indices).

- Block benchmarks do not predict training speed : measure your own training loop under torch.compile . Random inputs spread tokens evenly; a trained model has popular groups (the balancing bias counters that).

- Memory : compact activations [tokens, K·group_size] (gate and up) plus fp32 buffers [tokens, d_model] for y and dX .

- Changing group_size mid-training changes the number of groups and the buffer shapes (bias, subsample): it is a model change, not a setting.

- The example module counts group usage in its last forward call of the step; with gradient accumulation, accumulate lb_freq_now yourself.

## How to test

python test_eugen_sparse.py # GPU: everything; CPU: selection, subsample, balancing, plan TRITON_INTERPRET=1 python test_eugen_sparse.py # CPU: kernels vs reference in the Triton interpreter (fp32) python speed_check.py --compile # GPU: time dense vs sparse FFN block on YOUR card (our own figures: the model card above)

On a GPU the tests compare the kernel with the reference (y, dX, dW_gate, dW_up, dW_down) in fp32 and bf16, with several token chunks, run torch.library.opcheck and check torch.compile without graph breaks. How the kernels work: TECHNICAL.md .

## Files

eugen_sparse.py (library) · test_eugen_sparse.py · speed_check.py (a timing script to run on your own GPU) · example.py · TECHNICAL.md · LICENSE

# Announcing Project ProtoStar: Making Publicly Funded Science AI-Ready

- +10

An initiative bringing together universities, research organizations, industry, and the open science community to make publicly funded research easier to discover, reuse, and build upon.

Today, we're announcing Project ProtoStar , an initiative to unlock the potential of publicly funded scientific research by making datasets, models, and code more accessible and reusable, particularly for AI-driven research. ProtoStar brings together research institutions, industry, and the open science community to support the release of scientific artifacts in AI-ready, machine-actionable formats, and to demonstrate their value through a series of open challenges. The first challenge, hosted by Carnegie Mellon University , opens on November 2. See How to Participate below.

The initiative's founding partners include Carnegie Mellon University , Purdue University , Georgia Institute of Technology , Arizona State University , and The George Washington University , all working through the Open Forum for AI (OFAI) as the university coalition partner; the Astera Institute ; Hugging Face as the infrastructure partner; and the Open Research Community Accelerator (ORCA) , through its Fostering Innovation Network , as the community partner.

Participating organizations formalize their involvement through a memorandum of understanding supporting the release of suitable scientific datasets, models, and code in AI-ready formats on open infrastructure. Organizations interested in joining Project ProtoStar can reach out to protostar@orcaopen.org .

## Making publicly funded science more usable

The U.S. federal government invests approximately $190 billion annually in research and development , and federal policy increasingly expects the results to be shared publicly. Agencies such as the National Institutes of Health (NIH) and National Science Foundation (NSF) have strengthened public-access requirements for funded research publications and require researchers to plan for sharing the underlying data. Hugging Face is among the ten generalist repositories listed by NIH for sharing research data.

But making research publicly available does not automatically make it usable. Scientific datasets, models, and code are often scattered across incompatible systems, stored in static or legacy formats, or released without the documentation, metadata, and provenance needed to understand and reuse them. These limitations make it harder for researchers to build on existing work, and harder still for AI systems to discover, interpret, and combine scientific resources across disciplines.

Project ProtoStar aims to help close this gap by encouraging systematic sharing of publicly funded scientific artifacts in AI-ready formats, supported by open infrastructure and practical publishing guidance. It builds on efforts such as the National Cancer Institute's AI Data-Readiness Challenge and Hugging Face's guide to preparing public-sector data for AI . The goal is to make it easier for research organizations to meet existing public-access expectations while increasing the scientific value of the work they release.

The demand for reusable scientific resources is already evident. Hugging Face hosts more than 17,000 public datasets across core scientific domains , including genomics, protein design, chemistry, weather and climate, Earth observation, and astronomy. That figure approaches 29,000 when medicine and mathematics are included, alongside a comparable number of scientific models.

The pace of sharing is also accelerating. Researchers shared more than three times as many new science datasets on Hugging Face in the first nine months of 2026 as in the same period of 2025 , with growth remaining substantial even after excluding the largest individual uploader.

Figure 1. New public science datasets on Hugging Face per quarter, by domain (Q1 2023–Q3 2026). Counts datasets still public, by creation date. Source: Hugging Face Hub data, October 2026. Explore the data .

When organizations share research in reusable formats, the scientific community can build on it at scale. The 18 public repositories maintained by NIH's National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI) on Hugging Face have collectively received more than 11 million downloads, while NASA IMPACT's 27 repositories have received approximately 770,000 downloads, as of October 26, 2026. Documentation is also an important part of making these resources useful: 90% of dataset downloads on Hugging Face are from fully documented datasets .

Publicly available genomic data has proved important in contributing to research that further advances fields such as biological research; researchers at Hugging Face have been building on openly available scientific resources, including recent releases from HuggingFaceBio such as Carbon-A and Carbon-X . By releasing the resulting models, datasets, and tools openly, these efforts demonstrate how existing scientific resources can support new research that others can build upon.

This is the kind of activity that we are further catalyzing via Project ProtoStar through institutional policies adopted by participating orgs. As an early example of institutional commitment, CMU's Open Source Programs Office is encouraging its researchers to share suitable datasets, AI models, and other research outputs on Hugging Face, while recognizing the continued importance of domain-specific repositories.

## Open Science Challenges

Making scientific artifacts AI-ready is an important first step. We also want to demonstrate what researchers, developers, and the broader scientific community can accomplish when those resources are made available for reuse.

A central question for ProtoStar is: Can publicly funded scientific datasets, models, and code, released in AI-ready formats, be readily discovered, reused, combined, and extended to accelerate scientific discovery and public benefit?

To explore this, ProtoStar will organize a series of open challenges, each hosted by a participating research institution and built around scientific resources that the institution has released openly. The challenges have two complementary goals:

- Demonstrate scientific reuse. Produce concrete examples of researchers and developers building on publicly funded scientific artifacts, including applications that combine resources across institutions or disciplines.

- Learn what makes reuse possible. Identify technical barriers, documentation gaps, interoperability challenges, and successful practices that can inform future research infrastructure, funding decisions, and public policy.

The resulting projects and lessons learned will help build a practical evidence base for making publicly funded science more accessible and useful.

### The first challenge: Climate Risk Intelligence

Hosted by Carnegie Mellon University | November 2–13, 2026

The inaugural ProtoStar challenge invites participants to test whether AI can improve predictions of urban climate conditions using historical weather data from 210 U.S. cities. Building on research by Carnegie Mellon University , teams will use climate records through 2018 to predict actual conditions from 2019 to 2026, allowing their models to be evaluated against observed weather rather than hypothetical future scenarios.

Participants will forecast four indicators relevant to urban planning: average annual temperature, total annual precipitation, the hottest day of the year, and cooling degree days, a measure of demand for air conditioning. Their predictions will be compared against simple statistical baselines, including historical averages and linear trends, to assess whether AI approaches offer meaningful improvements in accuracy.

Beyond forecasting, participants will also propose a short climate adaptation policy idea informed by what they learned from the data. This component encourages teams to connect scientific analysis with practical public benefits, such as preparing cities for extreme heat, improving energy efficiency, or managing changing precipitation patterns.

Teams will submit a Hugging Face dataset with these outputs. Forecasting performance will be assessed through a public leaderboard measuring prediction errors against established baselines, while policy ideas will receive separate consideration. Final forecasting results will be published in early 2027, once the complete 2026 weather records are available.

Explore the CMU Climate Risk Intelligence Challenge

The CMU challenge is the first in this series. Other participating institutions will host their own challenges sequentially, each highlighting different publicly funded scientific resources and opportunities for reuse. Future challenges will be announced through the Project ProtoStar page on Hugging Face .

## How to Join Project ProtoStar

Whether you're an academic researcher, student, independent developer, or company building on open scientific infrastructure, ProtoStar offers opportunities to put publicly funded research to work and help us learn what is needed to make AI-ready open science more widely useful.

We also welcome universities, federal research agencies, national laboratories, nonprofits, and other research organizations interested in making their scientific resources more accessible and reusable. To explore participation or collaboration, reach out to protostar@orcaopen.org .

Our hope is that ProtoStar will make it easier for publicly funded scientific work to reach the people and tools that can build on it, while generating practical evidence about the infrastructure and practices needed to support open science at scale.

# Step 5 Preview

StepFun's flagship model for agentic work

600B total parameters · 27B active parameters · Up to 1M context

Introduction · Capabilities · Specifications · Performance · Deployment · Resources · License

## Introduction

Step 5 Preview is StepFun's flagship model for agentic work. It delivers frontier-level performance across software engineering and professional knowledge work, with particular strength in finance.

Step 5 Preview is a sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model with 600B total parameters and 27B active parameters. It supports up to 1 million tokens of context and accepts text, images, and video, enabling sustained reasoning and tool use across complex tasks.

## Key Capabilities

### Software Engineering

Step 5 Preview supports repository-level software engineering, frontend and visual development, and programming for devices. It can navigate large codebases, coordinate changes across files, run and verify code, and iterate on the results.

### Long-Horizon Agentic Execution

Step 5 Preview can carry out tasks that require repeated tool calls, execution, verification, and revision, drawing on long-context information throughout the workflow.

### Professional Knowledge Work

The model combines research, multimodal understanding, and tool use to analyze long documents, charts, screenshots, images, and video, and produce structured reports and analyses.

### A Focus on Finance

Step 5 Preview is particularly strong in financial tasks that combine quantitative reasoning with analysis of financial data and supporting documents.

## Model Specifications

## Performance

The following results summarize Step 5 Preview's performance across coding, agentic tasks, professional knowledge work, and finance.

### Evaluation Notes

- Recommended inference settings: temperature=1.0 , top_p=0.95 , top_k=0 .

- Step 5 Preview results shown above use the High reasoning setting.

- GDPval-AA v2.1 scores are based on results from Artificial Analysis as of September 20, 2026.

- DeepSWE v1.1 evaluations use the SWE-agent harness with temperature=1.0 and top_p=0.95 .

For evaluation context, methodology, and detailed case studies, see the Step 5 Preview Model Page .

## Deployment

Step 5 Preview can be served through an OpenAI-compatible API with vLLM or SGLang, or used for offline generation with the standalone Transformers implementation. The examples below cover FP8 and BF16 checkpoints.

Use a framework build that includes Step 5 Preview support, including the reasoning, tool-call, and speculative decoding features used in the serving commands.

### Deployment Configurations

DP, TP, and EP refer to data, tensor, and expert parallelism, respectively. TEP combines tensor and expert parallelism; DEP combines data and expert parallelism. These example configurations are sized for the deployments below. Actual memory requirements, usable context length, and concurrency vary with the checkpoint, inference framework, and KV cache allocation.

Deployment guides: vLLM · Transformers · SGLang · Send a Request

### vLLM

The examples below expose Step 5 Preview through an OpenAI-compatible API at port 18000 , with step5 as the model name used in requests.

#### Environment Setup

Pull the Step 5 Preview image and start an interactive container with GPU access:

docker pull vllm/vllm-openai:step-5-preview docker run -- rm -it \ --gpus all \ --ipc=host \ --network=host \ --volume " $HOME /.cache/huggingface:/root/.cache/huggingface" \ --entrypoint /bin/bash \ vllm/vllm-openai:step-5-preview

Run the serving commands below inside the container. If the checkpoint requires authentication, sign in with hf auth login before starting the server.

Choose one of the following parallel configurations for a single node with four B300 GPUs:

Make all four GPUs visible, then run the command for your chosen configuration:

export CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0,1,2,3

On B300 (Blackwell), the TEP4 and DEP4 commands select MegaMoE with --moe-backend deep_gemm_mega_moe . The TP4 command uses the default MoE backend, since MegaMoE requires expert parallelism.

vllm serve stepfun-ai/Step-5-Preview \ --host 0.0.0.0 \ --port 18000 \ --served-model-name "step5" \ --tensor-parallel-size 4 \ --data-parallel-backend mp \ --distributed-executor-backend mp \ --disable-custom-all-reduce \ --max-model-len 1048576 \ --max-num-batched-tokens 16384 \ --max-num-seqs 64 \ --gpu-memory-utilization 0.85 \ --enable-prefix-caching \ --spec-method mtp \ --spec-tokens 3 \ --reasoning-parser step5 \ --enable-auto-tool-choice \ --tool-call-parser step5

vllm serve stepfun-ai/Step-5-Preview \ --host 0.0.0.0 \ --port 18000 \ --served-model-name "step5" \ --tensor-parallel-size 4 \ --enable-expert-parallel \ --moe-backend deep_gemm_mega_moe \ --data-parallel-backend mp \ --distributed-executor-backend mp \ --disable-custom-all-reduce \ --max-model-len 1048576 \ --max-num-batched-tokens 16384 \ --max-num-seqs 64 \ --gpu-memory-utilization 0.85 \ --enable-prefix-caching \ --spec-method mtp \ --spec-tokens 3 \ --reasoning-parser step5 \ --enable-auto-tool-choice \ --tool-call-parser step5

vllm serve stepfun-ai/Step-5-Preview \ --host 0.0.0.0 \ --port 18000 \ --served-model-name "step5" \ --tensor-parallel-size 1 \ --data-parallel-size 4 \ --enable-expert-parallel \ --moe-backend deep_gemm_mega_moe \ --data-parallel-backend mp \ --distributed-executor-backend mp \ --disable-custom-all-reduce \ --max-model-len 1048576 \ --max-num-batched-tokens 16384 \ --max-num-seqs 64 \ --gpu-memory-utilization 0.85 \ --enable-prefix-caching \ --spec-method mtp \ --spec-tokens 3 \ --reasoning-parser step5 \ --enable-auto-tool-choice \ --tool-call-parser step5

For a single node with eight H200 GPUs, adapt one of the B300 commands above:

- Set CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0,1,2,3,4,5,6,7 .

- For TP8 or TEP8, set --tensor-parallel-size 8 . For DEP8, keep --tensor-parallel-size 1 and set --data-parallel-size 8 .

- For TEP8 or DEP8, retain --enable-expert-parallel and remove --moe-backend deep_gemm_mega_moe ; H200 (Hopper) uses the default MoE backend.

TP and TEP use DP=1; DEP uses TP=1. In all configurations, --max-num-seqs applies per DP rank. The 1M-token context limit covers input and output combined. If KV cache memory is insufficient, reduce --max-model-len or concurrency.

BF16 deployments require a BF16 checkpoint. Setting --dtype bfloat16 on the FP8 checkpoint does not convert its quantized weights to BF16.

Mount the BF16 checkpoint directory at the same path inside the container, then set MODEL to that path:

export MODEL= "<STEP5_BF16_MODEL_PATH>"

Retain the remaining serving arguments, including --served-model-name "step5" , --reasoning-parser step5 , and --tool-call-parser step5 .

TP16 / TEP16

For TP16, use the following arguments. For TEP16, also add --enable-expert-parallel on both nodes. Both configurations use DP=1.

Node 0:

--host 0.0.0.0 \ --port 18000 \ --tensor-parallel-size 16 \ --nnodes 2 \ --node-rank 0 \ --master-addr <NODE_0_IP>

DEP16

DEP16 uses TP=1 and distributes the experts across 16 data-parallel ranks, with eight ranks on each node. Use the same data-parallel address and RPC port on both nodes.

### Transformers

The standalone implementation converts checkpoints into shards for offline generation. With its dependencies installed, run the following commands from the inference/ directory:

cd inference

Use separate checkpoints and output directories for FP8 and BF16. Conversion preserves the source dtype, and generation runs offline without an API server.

Convert the FP8 checkpoint once, then launch eight local processes for TP8 / EP8 generation:

export STEP5_FP8_CHECKPOINT= "<FP8_CHECKPOINT_DIRECTORY>" export STEP5_FP8_OUT= "<FP8_SHARD_OUTPUT_DIRECTORY>" python3 convert.py \ --checkpoint " $STEP5_FP8_CHECKPOINT " \ --tp-size 8 --ep-size 8 --check-only python3 convert.py \ --checkpoint " $STEP5_FP8_CHECKPOINT " \ --out-dir " $STEP5_FP8_OUT " \ --tp-size 8 --ep-size 8 torchrun --standalone --nproc-per-node=8 generate.py \ --tp-dir " $STEP5_FP8_OUT /tp8" --ep-size 8 \ --prompt "Please introduce tensor parallelism." \ --max-new-tokens 128

For TP16 / EP16 generation across two nodes, first convert the BF16 checkpoint into 16 shards. Make the resulting tp16/ and tokenizer_files/ directories accessible to both nodes:

export STEP5_BF16_CHECKPOINT= "<BF16_CHECKPOINT_DIRECTORY>" export STEP5_BF16_OUT= "<BF16_SHARD_OUTPUT_DIRECTORY>" python3 convert.py \ --checkpoint " $STEP5_BF16_CHECKPOINT " \ --tp-size 16 --ep-size 16 --check-only python3 convert.py \ --checkpoint " $STEP5_BF16_CHECKPOINT " \ --out-dir " $STEP5_BF16_OUT " \ --tp-size 16 --ep-size 16

Then run the command below on each node, using the same MASTER_ADDR , MASTER_PORT , and shard output path. Set NODE_RANK=0 on node 0 and NODE_RANK=1 on node 1:

export STEP5_BF16_OUT= "<BF16_SHARD_OUTPUT_DIRECTORY>" export MASTER_ADDR= "<NODE_0_REACHABLE_IP_OR_HOSTNAME>" export MASTER_PORT=29500 export NODE_RANK=0 # Set to 1 on node 1. torchrun --nnodes=2 --nproc-per-node=8 \ --node-rank= " $NODE_RANK " \ --master-addr= " $MASTER_ADDR " \ --master-port= " $MASTER_PORT " \ generate.py \ --tp-dir " $STEP5_BF16_OUT /tp16" --ep-size 16 \ --prompt "Please introduce tensor parallelism." \ --max-new-tokens 128

This launches 16 processes across the two nodes, matching the 16-shard checkpoint and --ep-size 16 . The two-node launch uses a shared rendezvous address rather than --standalone .

BF16 validation: The full BF16 convert.py → generate.py --tp-dir file-shard workflow has not yet been validated end to end. The reference implementation has validated checkpoint names and shapes, BF16 small-model conversion, loading and generation, and full-model streaming-weight inference.

### SGLang

Pull the Step 5 Preview SGLang Docker image:

docker pull lmsysorg/sglang:step-5-preview

Then, launch the server using the configuration for your hardware. For more optimized configurations, including MegaMoE, attention data parallelism and HiCache, see the SGLang Cookbook for Step 5 Preview .
